what: Macy’s operates department stores. It runs the Macy’s chain, the upmarket Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury beauty shops, selling clothing, cosmetics, homeware and accessories. It owns a great deal of the real estate its stores sit on, which matters more to the investment case than the retailing does.
customers: American shoppers, through roughly five hundred stores and its websites. Bloomingdale’s serves a distinctly wealthier customer than the Macy’s nameplate.
money: Mid-market department stores and e-commerce, including the smaller-format off-mall stores.
Upmarket department stores, which have performed considerably better than the core chain.
Beauty speciality stores, plus credit card revenue and licensing income.
moat: Macy’s genuine assets are the Bloomingdale’s brand, the credit card income stream, and the property. Many of its stores sit on land worth more than the retailing operation inside them, particularly the flagship locations. The department store format itself has no moat at all, which is why the company’s strategy is to shrink it deliberately.
risks: Revenue has fallen every year shown, from $25.4B to $22.6B, and the department store format has been in structural decline for two decades.
Ten analysts average a $23.70 target against a $23.75 price, implying no upside at all. Analysts rarely publish flat targets, so this reflects genuine scepticism rather than caution.
Reported debt of about $5.6B includes lease obligations and is set against $1.2B of cash.
The reported free cash flow of $1.4B is flattered by capital spending cut to $347M, which cannot continue indefinitely without the stores deteriorating.
Closing stores releases cash once but removes revenue permanently, so the strategy improves the balance sheet while shrinking the business.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 8.7 times earnings, 0.27 times sales and 3.6 times EV/EBITDA, prices that assume continued decline.
Free cash flow of about $1.4B against a $6.2B market value is a very large yield, and it funds both the dividend and buybacks.
The owned real estate provides a floor under the valuation that pure retailers do not have, and monetising individual sites has been a reliable source of cash.
Bloomingdale’s and Bluemercury have been growing while the core chain shrinks, and together they are a meaningful share of profit.
Closing the weakest locations mechanically improves the margin of what remains, which is the clearest lever management holds.
watch: Comparable sales at the Macy’s nameplate excluding closures, and capital spending. Shrinking profitably is a legitimate strategy, but only if the remaining stores are maintained and the core brand stops losing customers.
view: The mistake people make with Macy’s is arguing about whether department stores have a future. They do not, or at least not many of them, and management broadly agrees — the strategy is to close the weakest locations, invest in the better ones, and grow Bloomingdale’s and Bluemercury. The real question is narrower and more interesting: is a deliberately shrinking retailer with valuable real estate and a large cash flow worth more than $6.2 billion? That is an arithmetic question, not a retail one.

Start with the cash, and be sceptical about it. Reported free cash flow of $1.4 billion against a $6.2 billion market value is a 22% yield, which would be extraordinary if it were sustainable. It is partly not. Operating cash flow of $1.76 billion is real, but capital expenditure has been cut to $347 million, which for a chain of five hundred large stores is maintenance-only spending at best. You cannot run department stores on that forever without customers noticing the carpets. A more honest normalised figure is meaningfully lower, and anyone underwriting the headline yield is underwriting an unsustainable capital spending level.

The real estate is the genuine support, and it is why this is a different proposition from Kohl’s. Macy’s owns land and buildings — including flagship locations — that in several cases are worth more than the retailing conducted inside them. That gives the equity a floor that does not depend on anyone’s view of apparel trends, and it has provided a reliable stream of one-off cash as individual sites are sold. The catch, which activists repeatedly discover, is that monetising it properly means closing stores, which removes revenue, which makes the remaining business smaller and the overheads harder to cover. There is no clean way to separate the property from the operations.

So the honest verdict: at 8.7 times earnings, 0.27 times sales and 3.6 times EV/EBITDA, this is priced for decline and you are being paid a large cash return to wait while the decline is managed. That can work very well — shrinking profitably while buying back stock is a legitimate way to compound per-share value — and the fact that ten analysts see exactly zero upside tells you nobody is excited, which is usually a better starting point than the opposite. But it requires management discipline over many years, and the first sign of trouble will be the Macy’s nameplate’s comparable sales continuing to fall after the closures are stripped out. Bloomingdale’s is the part of this company with an actual future; watch whether it grows fast enough to matter.
bull: Closures and buybacks shrink the business while growing value per share, real estate sales keep funding the return, and Bloomingdale’s grows into a meaningful share of profit.
bear: Core comparable sales keep falling after closures, capital spending has to normalise upward, and the cash yield that looked like 22% turns out to be half that against a declining revenue base.
